description: Hi! We’re Maria and Riddhi, and this is our first hackathon! We’re building a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer to make learning about space fun through interactive missions and challenges. We’re interested in coding, AI, game development, and space exploration. We’d love to team up with people who enjoy UI/UX design, animation, game development, or space science. Most importantly, we’re looking for people who are excited to learn, share ideas, and build something fun together!
summary:
What would it take to make the Moon your home? We built MOONBOUND, a browser-based game where young players find out by becoming astronauts themselves.

Through nine missions spelling MOONBOUND, players launch a rocket, land at the lunar south pole, search for frozen water, and build their own outpost. Along the way, they grow food, connect power systems, and keep their crew supplied with oxygen and water.

Real solar-flare records from NASA’s DONKI database inspire simulated storms that interrupt life at the base. Players must decide: stop working and take shelter, spend materials on shielding, or risk more radiation to keep going. The game explains the science behind these choices and where we have simplified it for gameplay.

MOONBOUND addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by giving children a chance to try, make mistakes, and discover what works. We want players to leave with more than space facts; we want them to understand how their decisions help keep a crew safe, and feel excited to explore further.

GitHub Link: https://github.com/mariamalik2105/MOONBOUND
details:
What we built

MOONBOUND is a browser-based lunar exploration and base-building game that lets children experience the challenges of becoming an astronaut. We wanted players to discover space science through actions they could see and control: launching a rocket, landing safely, finding water, and building a place where their crew can live.

The game follows nine phases that spell MOONBOUND: Mission Prep, Orbit, Outbound, Navigation, Bootdown, Outpost, Uncover, Network, and Development. Players begin by packing supplies and flying to the Moon. After landing at the lunar south pole, they explore on foot or by rover, scan rocks, collect ice, and construct their outpost.

Each mission introduces something the base needs, including solar power, batteries, oxygen generation, water recycling, communication, and food production. Players complete hands-on activities such as connecting electrical wires, aiming a radio dish, cleaning dusty panels, and tending crops. Completing missions unlocks blueprints and rewards, while the growing base makes their progress visible.

How NASA data becomes part of the game

One of MOONBOUND’s central features is its use of real solar-flare records from NASA’s DONKI space-weather database. When the service is available, the game retrieves recent records. Otherwise, it uses archived real events, clearly labeled so players know which they are seeing.

These records drive simulated radiation storms. Before a storm arrives, players have time to decide how to respond. Taking shelter reduces exposure but pauses work. Adding regolith shielding costs building materials. Continuing to work allows progress but increases radiation exposure in the game.

We wanted these choices to feel meaningful: protecting the crew, conserving supplies, and developing the base can pull players in different directions.

NASA radiation-protection guidance and published radiation measurements provide scientific context. However, MOONBOUND is an educational game, not a radiation simulator. Storm doses, shielding effects, and the connection between each flare and an in-game storm are simplified and explained to players. An optional Science Log provides further information and source links without interrupting play.

Why we think it matters

The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge gave us an opportunity to make mission planning something children can experience for themselves. A player might understand that astronauts need electricity, but building a solar panel, connecting a battery, and watching the base depend on that system makes the idea more concrete.

Our intended impact is to encourage curiosity, problem-solving, and an understanding of how lunar life-support systems depend on one another. We want children to feel comfortable experimenting, seeing the consequences, and trying again. Classroom playtesting is a next step so we can assess whether the instructions are clear and what players actually learn.

What makes MOONBOUND creative

MOONBOUND combines an arcade-style journey to the Moon with an open lunar outpost that players develop themselves. The nine-letter mission structure gives the adventure a clear beginning and progression, while repeatable base jobs give players reasons to return after completing the campaign.

Science is built into the decisions rather than presented only as questions to answer. Dust affects solar panels, crops need care, and storm protection comes with a cost. Astronaut specialists, companions, cosmetic rewards, and mission celebrations add personality and help make the experience inviting.

Players can also join multiplayer rooms with up to four crew members to explore and build together. Shared structures are synchronized, while a fully shared, server-managed resource economy remains a future improvement.

Tools and development

We developed MOONBOUND using React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, with a custom HTML5 Canvas engine for the main 2D game. Three.js supports 3D previews, and the Web Audio API generates sound effects.

The backend uses Node.js, Express, and Socket.IO for server functionality and multiplayer. Progress is saved locally through IndexedDB, with JSON import and export for backups. Automated tests use Node.js’s built-in test runner to check game rules, resource calculations, storms, saves, and server validation.

The game runs in a browser using a keyboard, mouse, or trackpad, without specialized hardware.

Design choices we considered

We focused on making the game approachable without removing the need to think. Short instructions, contextual controls, progress indicators, and hints help players understand their next action. Scientific explanations appear in layers, allowing curious players to explore further without requiring everyone to read long passages.

We also considered reliable access, fair rewards, and scientific transparency. Archived events keep the game playable when live data is unavailable. Rewards are earned through play, with no loot boxes or timers that punish players for leaving. Throughout development, we aimed to balance an enjoyable adventure with an honest explanation of the science behind it.
